# Conservative Party policy on rural, environmental, and agricultural

**Paris Accord / Net Zero / Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS)**\
 We believe that current climate policies are a distraction from real opportunities to protect and improve the environment. There is no climate emergency. We will end all climate-focused taxes, subsidies, and regulations. Laws/agreements like the Paris Accord, Zero Carbon Act, and Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS) impose significant costs on everyday New Zealanders while not improving environmental outcomes, and they all need to go.\
 \
 **Food production and rural communities**\
 \
 We do not support any policy that encourages the conversion of productive pastoral and arable land into permanent or long-term carbon forestry. Our focus is supporting farmers to continue being the best food producers in the world.\
 \
 **Energy**\
 \
 The best way to secure a nations prosperity is through energy policy. It is the position of the Conservative party that energy needs to be abundant, reliable, and affordable. Renewables have their place but should not favoured over reliable base load supply.\
 Methane research and AgriZero\
 We do not support taxpayers' funds being used in this field of research. If private entities wish to continue in this field they can source funding elsewhere. \
 \
 **Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill**\
 \
 The Conservative Party does not support either the Planning Bill or Natural Environmental Bill in its current form. We agree the legislation is not a practical solution and is causing too many headaches for our primary producers.\
 We support revisiting this legislation to focus on improving environmental outcomes, making the legislation workable in a practical way, and to secure property owner rights.\
 \
 **Proposed Gene Technology Bill**\
 \
 We oppose the current government's move to end the long-standing restrictions placed on field trials and the release of genetically modified organisms. \
 We consider that this proposal will overturn a societal consensus and such a decision should not be made without society-wide buy-in.\
 We note that to justify this proposal National and Act have turned to climate scaremongering, claiming we need genetically engineered organisms to reduce agricultural greenhouse gas emissions.\
 We believe that this is an inappropriate use of technology—we should not be playing God and altering the natural makeup of organisms for no real environmental benefit—and these parties and their reliance on this\
 justification shows there is no real case for change.\
 \
 **Inflationary Burden**\
 \
 We have multiple policies to address the burden of inflation on the New Zealand people.\
 •    Reduce the size of government. We cannot continue the level of government spending.\
 •    Reduce taxation. The New Zealand citizen can spend their money far better than the government can.\
 •    Encourage self-reliance. Make use of New Zealand's fossil fuels and minerals (including our own oil refinery). Investigate the procurement of our own oil tankers, which secures oil transportation and adds to our floating storage capacity.\
 •    Bring back New Zealand manufacturing.

# Bureaucracy Policy

\
 **BUREAUCRATIC USURPATION OF GOVERNANCE.**\
 \
 Legislate to curtail unconstitutional bureaucratic power is a priority for the Conservative Party.\
 \
 All government departments are affected by a malaise that grows in direct proportion to the weakened will and authority of those elected to parliament. \
 \
 Bureaucrats, elements of the Judiciary, and unelected advisors at both national and local levels have increasingly chosen to usurp the democratic mandate of elected representatives and the people they serve.\
 \
 This subversion manifests through misleading or selectively framed advice to politicians, the deliberate obstruction of legitimate policy strategies emanating from Cabinet, and the routine overriding of lawmakers’ expectations and priorities.\
 \
 Rather than serving as neutral administrators, these institutions often advance their own ideological agendas – frequently at odds with the expressed will of the electorate.  The result is a profound frustration for those elected officials who seek to act in good faith on behalf of the public.  Instead of enabling effective governance, bureaucratic resistance functions as parasitic drag: a constant, hidden drain on national performance, economic vitality and societal well-being. \
 \
 What should be a smooth engine of progress is slowed and degraded by internal forces that answer to neither voter or results.

**WE ARE RULED BY UNELECTED BUREAUCRATS**

This is obvious at both local and national levels.

Part-time Mayors and Councillors are powerless against their highly-paid CEOs and staff (who may come with their own agendas).

At the national level, the Labour Party is only too happy to have Ministries staffed by ideological fellow-travellers, while the National Party gave up 30 years ago on doing anything about it.

**Elect the Conservative Party to Parliament, and we will:**

- Give Mayors the option to become full-time CEOs of their Council.  They would still be subject to the normal constraints of the law and of full Council.  Incoming Mayors could campaign on their suitability as CEO.  If you don't like what they do while in office - vote them out at the next election.

- At the national level, give Ministers wide powers to appoint senior civil servants (subject to the approval of the Prime Minister and Cabinet).

- At both local and national level, elected representatives should be given wide powers to sack staff who are incompetent, obstructive, or who take initiatives for which they clearly have no mandate.  Public sector pay is already 26% higher than in the private sector - civil servants should have the same job security as their private sector counterparts.

## **The highest civic virtue is accountability.**

# Child Protection (2026 campaign site)

## Full text (verbatim)

[Home](/) » [Policies](https://conservatives.org.nz/policies/) » Child Protection

# Protecting Our Children

# Our Commitment

The Conservative Party believes every child has the right to grow up safe from abuse, exploitation, violence, neglect and unnecessary harm.

Children are among the most vulnerable members of our society. Government, families, schools, health professionals and the justice system all have a responsibility to protect them.

Our policy is based on a simple principle:

**The safety, wellbeing and long-term interests of the child must come first.**

We will strengthen protections for children, support parents in their responsibility for their children, hold serious offenders accountable, and ensure government agencies act quickly and effectively when children are at risk.

## Stronger Protection from Sexual Offending

Sexual offending against children is among the most serious crimes in our society. The consequences for victims can last a lifetime, and sentencing should properly recognise the severity and lasting impact of these offences.

The Conservative Party will:

- Increase penalties for serious sexual offending against children.
- Ensure repeat child sexual offenders face significantly longer prison sentences.
- Review sentence reductions for the most serious sexual offences against children to ensure sentences properly reflect the seriousness of the offending.
- Improve monitoring and management of high-risk sexual offenders following their release.
- Strengthen resources for investigating online child exploitation and identifying offenders.
- Ensure victims and their families have timely access to counselling, trauma support and appropriate long-term assistance.

## Protect Children from Medical Harm

Children deserve particularly strong safeguards when medical treatment may have irreversible or lifelong consequences.

The Conservative Party believes significant medical interventions involving minors must be based on high-quality medical evidence, genuine medical necessity and rigorous standards of informed consent.

We will:

- Restrict elective and irreversible medical procedures intended to alter a child's sex characteristics or reproductive capabilities where there is no clear medical necessity.
- Require comprehensive and appropriately independent assessment before significant medical intervention relating to gender distress in minors.
- Ensure parents or legal guardians are appropriately involved in significant healthcare decisions affecting their children, subject to necessary safeguards for the child's safety and existing legal obligations.
- Require treatment and clinical practice involving minors to be based on high-quality evidence and robust informed-consent standards.
- Establish appropriate independent review and complaints mechanisms for significant treatment involving minors.

## Protect Childhood from Sexual Exploitation

Children should be able to grow and develop without being targeted for sexual exploitation, grooming or inappropriate sexualisation.

The Conservative Party will:

- Increase penalties for producing, possessing, distributing or commercially exploiting child sexual abuse material.
- Strengthen laws and enforcement against online grooming and sexual exploitation of children.
- Improve the ability of law enforcement agencies to identify and investigate online offenders.
- Expand education and practical resources for parents about online risks, grooming, sextortion and exploitation.
- Work with technology providers and relevant agencies to improve the detection and reporting of child sexual abuse material.

## Safe Schools

Every child deserves to feel safe at school and every parent should be able to expect that schools will provide a secure environment focused on education.

The Conservative Party supports schools that:

- Maintain safe, orderly and respectful learning environments.
- Take bullying and intimidation seriously.
- Protect students from harassment, sexual harassment and sexual violence.
- Respond quickly when a child's safety is threatened.
- Keep parents appropriately informed about significant matters affecting their children.
- Focus strongly on academic achievement and core educational outcomes.
- Ensure health and relationship education is age-appropriate, transparent to parents and focused on children's health, safety and wellbeing rather than political or ideological advocacy.

## Mental Health and Trauma Support

Children experiencing mental distress, abuse or trauma should receive timely, professional and compassionate assistance.

The Conservative Party will:

- Improve access to appropriately qualified child psychologists and mental health professionals.
- Recognise the important role of parents and guardians in supporting children's mental health and involve them appropriately in assessment and treatment, subject to safeguards where a child's safety may be at risk.
- Reduce waiting times for youth mental health services.
- Expand specialist support for children who have experienced sexual abuse, violence or other serious trauma.
- Invest in early intervention where evidence shows it can prevent more serious long-term harm.

## Supporting Strong Families

Strong, stable and loving families provide one of the greatest protections available to children.

Government should support good parents rather than unnecessarily replacing or undermining their role.

The Conservative Party will:

- Support practical parenting education and family assistance.
- Strengthen early intervention when abuse, serious neglect or exploitation is identified.
- Improve coordination between families, schools, healthcare providers, Police and child protection agencies.
- Ensure agencies share critical information appropriately when a child is genuinely at risk.
- Prioritise the safety and wellbeing of children while respecting the rights and responsibilities of loving parents and guardians.

## Child Trafficking and Commercial Sexual Exploitation

New Zealand must take a zero-tolerance approach to the trafficking, sale and commercial sexual exploitation of children.

The Conservative Party will:

- Increase resources for investigating suspected child trafficking and organised exploitation.
- Strengthen cooperation between Police, Customs, immigration authorities and international enforcement agencies.
- Ensure severe penalties apply to those who traffic, procure, sell or commercially sexually exploit children.
- Strengthen measures to identify and protect children at risk of trafficking or exploitation.
- Provide appropriate long-term support for children rescued from trafficking or commercial sexual exploitation.

## Protecting Children from Inappropriate Sexualised Content

Children should not be deliberately targeted with sexually explicit or developmentally inappropriate material.

The Conservative Party will:

- Review standards governing sexually explicit or highly sexualised material directed towards children.
- Ensure material provided through schools and publicly funded children's programmes is age-appropriate.
- Support parents' right to know what sexuality and relationship material is being presented to their children.
- Require clear parental transparency around programmes dealing with sensitive sexual or gender-related subjects.
- Apply consistent child-safety standards regardless of the political, social or ideological viewpoint associated with the material.

## Our Principle

**Children deserve protection, parents deserve respect, victims deserve justice, and serious offenders must be held accountable.**

The Conservative Party will put the safety and wellbeing of New Zealand children at the centre of decisions affecting their lives.

# CONSERVATIVE PARTY "CLIMATE" POLICY

## **Background**

"Climate" policies (for example "Net Zero", new energy taxes, restrictions on fossil fuel use) are not based on science, but on the conjuring up of scary scenarios ("Global Warming").  Even the chief global body (the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) now admits that the scariest scenarios (upon which all "climate" policies are based) are not supported by the data.

The USA, China, India, the OPEC countries - and many others - are not bound by "climate" policies.  Closer to home, the state of Queensland has abandoned "climate" policies (likely soon followed by the rest of Australia).

In Europe we see the fruits of "climate" policies.  Germany - long the industrial powerhouse of Europe - is committing industrial suicide as a result of dogmatic adherence to "climate" policies.  In the UK, we can also see how the ideology of "climate" inflicts economic harm: for example North Sea oil and gas taxes (royalties) are now at a crippling 75% (in the name of "climate"), causing BP to sell off their interests there.  "Climate" ideology directly causes harm: for example the National Health Service in England has recently prioritised the restriction of air conditioning above patient outcomes (as a result many blood samples have had to be destroyed, and blood tests will have to be re-done).

Health, wealth, and economic growth are reliant on cheap and abundant energy.  This has not changed since the days of the Industrial Revolution.

The driving idea behind all "climate" policies is not "saving the planet", but economic and social control.

A striking feature of "climate" policies (for example higher food and energy prices) is that they hurt the poor the most.

## **Our Policies**

Conservate Party continue to say that New Zealand should leave the Paris Agreement (and any other international agreements relating to "climate").

All taxes and restrictions on fossil fuels which are based on "climate" ideology should be scrapped.

New Zealand should encourage the cheap and abundant supply of all kinds of energy.  No form of energy, however, should enjoy state subsidy.

## All legislation and regulations based on "climate" ideology should be repealed or withdrawn.

All departments (or parts of departments) in government which deal with "climate" policies should be scrapped.  All "climate" policies followed by government departments and state owned enterprises should be withdrawn.

The result will be reduced food and energy prices (especially important for the those who are already struggling day to day), and a much more welcoming environment for agriculture, industry and transport.  All households and businesses will benefit.  And of course, lower taxes and fewer regulations.

# Energy

# We need access to cheap, reliable, and abundant energy

No country has ever achieved significant economic growth without access to cheap, reliable, and abundant energy. We are no different. This has been the case for every country since the Industrial Revolution.

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| | | | | --- | --- | | | | | --- | | Renewables such as solar or wind have a part to play but cannot, and should not, be solely relied upon for electricity supply. - Solar and wind output can fluctuate extremely. This requires alternate generation to be already online in reserve (generators cannot turn on and off instantaneously). There is a mismatch between high solar production during the middle of the day when demand is lower, and peak electricity demand in the evening when supply is low. - Windmills, which are a blight on the landscape, are problematic too. The wind doesn’t always blow, and rotating blades are a danger to flying wildlife. Environmental concerns such as the disposal of old turbine blades and potential asbestos exposure are yet to be resolved. - Some turbines use asbestos for the turbine braking material linings, which is a significant health hazard to people in proximity. This danger is still not fully assessed in New Zealand. **New Zealand uses a Marginal Cost Pricing Model**: This wholesale spot market sets the price for all electricity by the most expensive generation at any one time. Regardless of where the power comes from, all generators get paid that same high price. - The Conservative Party would separate generation companies from retailing. This would allow retailers to source wholesale electricity from any provider. This incentivises competition, reducing electricity prices for homes and businesses. **Underinvestment in New Generation:** Generation capacity growth has been slow. The Conservative Party would encourage investment in new generation to provide “base load” supply. - Encourage natural gas power generation once our own commercial supply of gas is established, providing base load supply when hydro lakes are low, or when wholesale energy prices are high. Resulting in reduced wholesale prices. - Encourage the expansion of geothermal generation. - Encourage new clean coal generation. | | |

# Health (2026 campaign site)

## Full text (verbatim)

[Home](/) » [Policies](https://conservatives.org.nz/policies/) » Health

# Health

\
 **1. Hospital Waiting Times Must Be the Number-One Priority**\
 The central problem is not simply how much New Zealand spends on healthcare. It is whether patients receive care in a reasonable timeframe.\
 The policy should therefore measure success through patient outcomes and access, including:\
 •    Elective surgery waiting times.\
 •    Specialist appointment waiting times.\
 •    Diagnostic delays.\
 •    Cancer treatment access.\
 •    Emergency Department turnaround.\
 •    Hospital admission delays.\
 •    Delayed discharge.\
 Health NZ has reported more than 1.3 million Emergency Department presentations in 2023/24, while nearly 2.1 million people attended first specialist assessments.\
 \
 The Conservative approach should be to focus additional resources on increasing the number of patients treated rather than simply increasing expenditure.\
 \
 **2. Where The Money Will Come From**\
 The policy does not need to begin with a promise of substantially higher taxes.\
 Budget 2026 provides more than $5.8 billion in new Vote Health operating funding over the forecast period, including a further $1.37 billion annual uplift for Health NZ’s frontline cost pressures.\
 Total Vote Health funding for 2026/27 is approximately $33.031 billion, with Health NZ funding for services of approximately $27.154 billion.\
 **The Conservative argument should therefore be:**\
 New Zealand is already spending a very large amount on healthcare. The first question should be whether we are getting the maximum possible healthcare from the money we already spend.\
 \
 Funding for the waiting-time programme would come from five sources.\
 A. Reduce unnecessary bureaucracy\
 Identify administrative expenditure that does not directly contribute to patient care.\
 Savings should be redirected towards:\
 •    Doctors.\
 •    Nurses.\
 •    Allied health.\
 •    Theatre staff.\
 •    Emergency Department staff.\
 •    Diagnostic services.\
 B. Improve procurement\
 Use national purchasing power to reduce unnecessary variation and duplication in:\
 •    Medical equipment.\
 •    Supplies.\
 •    Technology.\
 •    Pharmaceuticals and services.\
 •    External contracts.\
 Savings should be retained within the health system and redirected to frontline care.\
 C. Increase productivity\
 Hospitals should make better use of:\
 •    Operating theatres.\
 •    Diagnostic equipment.\
 •    Hospital beds.\
 •    Clinical staff.\
 •    Extended-hours capacity where clinically appropriate.\
 The objective is to treat more patients using the infrastructure already available.\
 D. Purchase private capacity where it makes financial sense\
 Government should compare the cost of creating additional public capacity with the cost of purchasing treatment from an accredited private provider.\
 If an existing private operating theatre and specialist team can treat a patient sooner at a competitive cost, that capacity should be used.\
 E. Targeted additional investment\
 Where genuine workforce or infrastructure shortages remain, additional funding should be provided — but linked to measurable outcomes.\
 More funding must produce more healthcare.\
 \
 3. The Healthcare Workforce Challenge\
 New Zealand has a genuine workforce challenge, but the situation is more complicated than simply saying there are not enough health workers.\
 Health NZ’s current workforce analysis estimates a nursing shortage of approximately 2,250, although Health NZ explicitly cautions that workforce estimates have limitations and should not be treated as fixed targets.\
 For doctors, Health NZ reports approximately 21,800 FTE doctors, with around 10,800 working in hospitals and 11,000 in the community.\
 New Zealand has historically had limited domestic medical training capacity. There were 614 medical school places at the start of 2025, with additional capacity being introduced.\
 \
 Conservative Response\
 We should not simply attempt to recruit our way out of the problem.\
 We should:\
 1. Train more New Zealanders.\
 2. Retain more New Zealand-trained professionals.\
 3. Improve working conditions and career development.\
 4. Expand specialist and regional training.\
 5. Recruit overseas professionals where genuine shortages remain.\
 6. Make better use of the workforce we already have.\
 \
 Immigration – A Balanced Approach\
 Immigration should be discussed carefully because New Zealand currently depends significantly on internationally trained health professionals.\
 In 2024, internationally qualified nurses represented 42.6% of the nursing workforce.\
 Health NZ notes that internationally qualified nurses have helped ease workforce pressure, while also identifying retention and specialist workforce challenges.\
 International medical graduates represented approximately 42.1% of practising doctors in 2025.\
 Therefore, an immediate blanket reduction in health-worker immigration could make workforce shortages worse.\
 \
 The Conservative Position\
 Controlled immigration, targeted to genuine national need.\
 We should:\
 1.    Prioritise doctors, nurses and other critical professionals where genuine shortages exist.\
 2.    Maintain New Zealand registration and competency standards. -Reduce unnecessary delays in recognising appropriately qualified professionals.\
 3.    Increase domestic health training.\
 4.    Improve retention of New Zealand-trained professionals.\
 5.    Regularly review immigration settings against workforce demand and infrastructure capacity.\
 6.    Avoid relying on permanent high levels of overseas recruitment as a substitute for domestic workforce planning.\
 \
 New Zealand should recruit the health professionals it genuinely needs while building the domestic workforce required for the future.\
 \
 5. Retention Is as Important as Recruitment\
 Recruiting more doctors and nurses is only part of the solution.\
 The Medical Council has reported a significant difference in retention between locally and overseas-trained doctors. Its analysis found that only 28.7% of overseas-trained doctors remained in New Zealand after five years, compared with 84.9% of locally trained doctors in the cited cohorts.\
 This reinforces the need to:\
 •    Improve working conditions.\
 •    Reduce unnecessary administration.\
 •    Provide career development.\
 •    Improve access to specialist training.\
 Support rural and regional healthcare workers.\
 •    Improve leadership and workplace culture.\
 •    Make New Zealand an attractive long-term place to practise.\
 Keeping a trained doctor or nurse is often more valuable than repeatedly\
 recruiting replacements.\
 \
 6. Emergency Department Turnaround\
 Emergency Departments are a critical part of the waiting-time problem.\
 Reducing ED delays requires action across the whole health system.\
 The policy should therefore address:\
 Before ED\
 •    Better access to GPs.\
 •    Community pharmacy services.\
 •    Community healthcare.\
 •    Appropriate urgent-care services.\
 Inside ED\
 •    Faster triage.\
 •    Faster diagnostics.\
 •    Appropriate streaming of patients.\
 •    Faster specialist review.\
 •    Better use of clinical staff.\
 After ED\
 •    Faster admission to hospital wards.\
 •    Better bed management.\
 •    Faster discharge when clinically appropriate.\
 •    Stronger links with community and aged-care services.\
 The goal is not simply to make patients move through ED faster.\
 The goal is to remove the blockages that cause patients to wait unnecessarily.\
 \
 7. Public and Private Healthcare Partnership\
 New Zealand already has both public and private healthcare infrastructure.\
 The Conservative policy should make better use of both.\
 Where a patient is waiting for surgery and an accredited private provider has capacity, Government should be able to purchase that treatment where it is clinically appropriate and financially competitive.\
 This avoids unnecessary duplication of infrastructure.\
 Instead of asking:\
 “Is this a public or private hospital?” the question should be:\
 “Can this patient be treated safely, sooner and at a reasonable cost?”\
 \
 8. Domestic Training Strategy\
 Long-term workforce security requires more New Zealand-trained professionals.\
 The policy should support:\
 Doctors\
 •    More medical school places.\
 •    More postgraduate training positions.\
 •    More regional training.\
 •    Incentives for shortage specialties.\
 •    Rural and provincial training pathways.\
 Nurses\
 •    More nursing training capacity where shortages exist.\
 •    Better student retention.\
 •    Improved transition from education into employment.\
 •    Specialist nursing pathways.\
 •    Nurse practitioner development.\
 Allied Health\
 Expand training and workforce planning for professions such as:\
 •    Medical imaging.\
 •    Anaesthetic technicians.\
 •    Physiotherapy.\
 •    Occupational therapy.\
 •    Pharmacy.\
 •    Rehabilitation.\
 •    Diagnostic and technical services.\
 Health NZ’s workforce plan already identifies the need to expand placement capacity for several specialist and allied health professions and establish rural training hubs.\
 \
 9. Accountability\
 Additional funding should never be provided without accountability.\
 Health providers should publish:\
 •    Waiting-list numbers.\
 •    Average waiting times.\
 •    ED turnaround times.\
 •    Number of procedures completed.\
 •    Theatre utilisation.\
 •    Cancellation rates.\
 •    Staff vacancy rates.\
 •    Patient outcomes.\
 Funding should increasingly be linked to delivery and outcomes.\
 Key principle:\
 If taxpayers provide more money, patients should receive more healthcare.\
 \
 10. The Conservative Health Model\
 Our model can be summarised in six steps:\
 1. PRIORITISE\
 Put waiting lists and Emergency Departments first.\
 2. REPRIORITISE\
 Move money from unnecessary administration to frontline care.\
 3. EXPAND\
 Train more New Zealand doctors, nurses and healthcare professionals.\
 4. RETAIN\
 Keep experienced professionals in New Zealand.\
 5. USE CAPACITY\
 Use public, private and community providers where they deliver safe, timely and cost-effective care.\
 6. MEASURE\
 Publish results and hold providers accountable.\
 \
 **Final Policy Message**\
 New Zealand does not necessarily need to spend endlessly more to fix healthcare. It needs to use the money and workforce it already has better, remove unnecessary barriers, expand domestic training, retain skilled professionals and use every available source of safe healthcare capacity.\
 Where additional investment is genuinely required, it should be targeted and linked to measurable results.\
 The Conservative Party’s promise is not simply to spend more on health.\
 It is to deliver more healthcare for every dollar spent.\
 Patients First.\
 Faster Treatment.\
 Stronger Workforce.\
 Less Bureaucracy.\
 Better Value.\
 \
 \

# Immigration (2026 campaign site)

## Full text (verbatim)

[Home](/) » [Policies](https://conservatives.org.nz/policies/) » Immigration

# Immigration

**We very much welcome hard-working immigrants who can support themselves and their families, and who share our values.**

They leave their old lives behind, bringing their much-needed skills, their families, their life savings (for example, they may sell their former properties), and they pay tax - all in all making a major contribution to the fabric of New Zealand society.

However, if our population grows faster than our stock of social goods (medical professionals, hospital beds, school places, housing, etc.) then all New Zealanders become poorer.

**Background**

We see in many countries overseas the fruits of poorly controlled or managed immigration.

As a small island country, distant from the world's main population centres, New Zealand can avoid these problems - but only if we keep up our guard.

Canada - a country like ours that welcomes immigrants - stands as a perfect example of how not to do things.  As a result of decades of poorly managed immigration, they now have: strictly rationed healthcare; many Canadians unable to afford a home; a high penetration of organised crime from overseas; high rates of immigration fraud; low productivity (through over-reliance on imported unskilled labour); and higher rates of youth unemployment.

In New Zealand there appear to be an increasing number of overseas drivers of goods vehicles who may not be properly qualified (observation).

The issue of residence visas based on money alone ("golden" visas) is a magnet for organised criminals (New Zealand is no different in this regard to other countries).

New Zealand has a deservedly poor reputation among good quality migrants, because we are always changing the rules without notice (bringing uncertainty, wasted time, and expense to them).

**Our Policies**

The granting of work and residence visas should be adjusted away from unskilled and semi-skilled workers (and their dependents) towards skilled professionals and entrepreneurs.  This should be based on a stable points system (as is the case in other countries), with only minor changes over time (and signalled in advance).

With the exception of these skilled migrants, net immigration to New Zealand should be capped based on a broad measure of social goods (such as housing stock, the number of medical professionals, hospital beds, school places).  If our social goods are not increasing, net immigration of unskilled and semi-skilled workers and their dependents should be zero.

Immigrant drivers of goods vehicles should sit the appropriate driving licence test in New Zealand before they are allowed to drive on our roads.  If they fail twice, they should be repatriated at the sponsoring employer's expense.

More rigorous cross-checking and audits of supporting documents used in residence, work, and student visa applications should be introduced.  Restrictions should be placed on immigration from countries known or discovered to have high rates of fraud in this regard.

The staffing and processes used in the granting of residence and work visas should be regularly reviewed and audited from the ground up (immigration departments overseas have been known to be infiltrated by organised criminals).

The practice of issuing residence visas based on money alone ("golden" visas) should cease.

Overall - as in other fields prone to fraud - it is important that New Zealand is not seen as a "soft touch" by undesirable immigrants.

Lastly, GDP (gross domestic product) should routinely be expressed by the government on a *per capita* basis (and after adjusting for inflation).  This is a better measure of whether we are becoming richer or poorer.

Conservatives NZ stands for practical, common-sense government founded on personal responsibility, strong families, individual freedom, equal treatment and respect for New Zealand’s democratic traditions.

### Strong families and communities

Strong families are the foundation of a healthy society. Our policies encourage personal responsibility, stable families and communities that care for their children, elderly, vulnerable and disadvantaged.

### Freedom and individual responsibility

New Zealanders should be free to express their views, practise their beliefs, peacefully assemble and make responsible choices about their own lives.

Every New Zealander should have the same rights, responsibilities and opportunities under the law.

### A strong and productive economy

New Zealand needs an economy that rewards work, enterprise, innovation and investment.

We support tax and regulatory settings that encourage businesses to grow, young New Zealanders to build their futures here, and our country to make responsible use of its natural resources.

### Safe communities and equal justice

The first responsibility of government is to protect its people.

We support properly resourced police, meaningful consequences for serious and repeat offending, support for victims, and a justice system that applies the law fairly and consistently.

### Protecting New Zealand’s future

We are committed to protecting New Zealand’s natural environment while ensuring environmental policy is practical, affordable and supported by credible evidence.

We want future generations to inherit a country that is safe, prosperous, democratic and united.

# Right to Life and Legal Recognition of the Unborn Child in the Third Trimester

**Policy principle**

The Conservative Party believes that every human life has inherent dignity and value. We recognise that legal protection for unborn life is an important matter of public discussion and that changes to the law should be developed carefully, transparently and with respect for both the unborn life and the health and rights of pregnant women. We will introduce legislation recognising an unborn child from the beginning of the third trimester, defined for the purposes of the legislation as 28 weeks gestation, as a distinct human life entitled to enhanced legal protection.

**Policy commitments**

1. **Legal personhood:** Introduce an Unborn Child (Legal Personhood and Rights) Act recognising an unborn child as a legal person from the last trimester, with rights and protections expressly defined by legislation.
2. **Right to life:** Establish the right to life of the unborn child as a fundamental legal interest that Parliament and the courts must take into account when interpreting and applying the law.
3. **Protection from unlawful harm:** Strengthen legal protections against the intentional unlawful killing, assault or injury of an unborn child.
4. **Protection of pregnant women:** Ensure that legislation does not criminalise a pregnant woman for the natural outcome of her pregnancy, miscarriage, or seeking necessary medical care. Establish clear protections for healthcare professionals providing lawful and necessary treatment.
5. **Support for mothers and families:** Expand practical support for women facing crisis pregnancies, including access to counselling, maternity care, financial assistance and adoption information, so that no woman feels compelled to end a pregnancy because she lacks support.

**Legislative objective**

The Conservative Party will seek to establish a coherent legal framework in which the unborn child is recognised as a human life deserving of legal protection, with clearly defined rights, responsibilities and safeguards. The legislation will expressly address how those rights interact with the rights and medical needs of the pregnant woman.

The Conservative Party recognises that an unplanned pregnancy can bring financial hardship, emotional distress, housing insecurity and uncertainty about the future. Women facing these circumstances deserve practical assistance, compassionate support and genuine choices.

We will establish a **Pregnancy and Family Support Programme** to help women who are pregnant and do not feel able or prepared to raise a child.

Our policy commitments are:

**1. Pregnancy Support Payment**

Provide eligible pregnant women experiencing financial hardship with targeted financial assistance during pregnancy to help meet essential costs, including food, maternity clothing, transport and medical appointments.

**2. Housing security**

Work with housing providers and community organisations to improve access to safe, temporary accommodation for pregnant women who are homeless, escaping violence or at risk of losing their housing.

**3. A dedicated pregnancy support service**

Establish a confidential service connecting pregnant women with practical assistance, independent counselling, maternity care, budgeting support, accommodation and relevant government benefits.

**4. Support for single mothers and families**

Improve access to parenting assistance, childcare, financial advice and community support, recognising that women should not face the costs and responsibilities of raising a child without help.

**6. Adoption and alternative care**

Ensure that women who do not wish or feel able to raise a child can access independent information about lawful adoption and other available care arrangements. Counselling must be non-coercive, and decisions must be made freely and with appropriate safeguards.

**7. Practical support beyond birth**

Provide eligible families with a clear pathway to ongoing assistance after childbirth, including access to health services, early childhood support, parenting programmes and financial assistance.

**Our commitment**

We believe that protecting unborn life must be accompanied by a commitment to support women in practical ways. We will work towards a New Zealand where a woman facing an unplanned pregnancy is not left to manage financial hardship, homelessness or fear alone, and where she has access to meaningful support to make an informed decision about her future.

# Press Release

FINANCE POLICY

 

Conservatives NZ are committed to urgently tackling the massive debt the Labour Green government imposed on young families of today and their children of tomorrow.

 

Conservatives will press for a flat tax rate for individuals and for companies.

 

Laffer Curve Theory demonstrates that lower taxation encourages full disclosure by individuals, small business and big companies. When a lower tax policy was applied in New Zealand during late 1980s, Treasury incomes did increase in the first year.

 

For competitive reasons, rates of income tax should be equal or lower than other countries such as Australia. Lower taxation rates encourage investment decisions based on the return rather than the tax benefit. Retention of capital will encourage entrepreneurs to start their own businesses and remain in NZ.

 

Corporation tax rate should be aligned with the top rate of income tax. Whether income or expenses are corporate or personal - because both taxed at the same rate – will significantly reduce administrative costs - such as "left pocket to right pocket" manoeuvres simply to reduce tax.

 

Lower company rates encourage companies to return to New Zealand, creating employment and elevating Tax revenue to Treasury. Collateral impact is the private sector prevailing over State control of commercial activity.

 

A lower rate of GST -12.5% is favoured.

 

 

TRADE

Australia and China remain New Zealand’s largest trading partners.

Affinity with Australia embraces 3 centuries ranging from sacrifice in war conflicts of the past; competition on the sports fields and mutually beneficial trade. 

However, it is to China, that we must accord a trade priority.

 

TRADE RELATIONS POLICY viz CHINA

New Zealand needs a very clear Foreign Affairs strategy that avoids criticising and impugning China’s “face” as the Australians have managed to do.

Over the last decade, New Zealand has become heavily involved with China, to an extent that special attention is required to maintain, support and grow the two-way trade mechanism between NZ and PRC.

Before Covid, Chinese in-bound tourism was a significant part of tourism, NZ’s second largest generator of revenue. University revenue streams have also been substantially reduced through loss of international student education fees

 

Economic damage on these two sectors has been exacerbated by Labour Green policy of isolating New Zealand to “Hermit” status while wider commercial damage caused by this current government’s failure to adequately address economic recovery.

New Zealand primary products exports are also very exposed to reliance on China.

 

Trade to China in forestry (log exports) agricultural, horticultural and fish has become “over-weight” dependent on China as an export destination.

Trade bureaucracy can have major non-tariff impacts – as many companies have experienced.  Delays that use up date codes, unusual food safety requirements and late documentation can impose crippling costs.

 

Foreign Affairs approach needs to be sensitive and well thought through, starting with a competitive, credible, nuanced, presentable Foreign Affairs Minister.

Recovery and preservations of these sectors of commercial activity with China, is a priority for the Conservative Party.

 

 

TARIFF BALANCE

Conservatives NZ is cognisant of the damage done to New Zealand’s self-sufficiency and manufacturing skill base and employment, as a result of tariff free access for imported goods.

Conservatives NZ will review all trade agreements.  A balance between open slather free access and Trump like self-protection tariffs at the other extreme, needs to be found.

 

FOREIGN AFFAIRS

Economic growth and regional stability are priorities of the Conservatives NZ.  Trade before War should be New Zealand’s axiom.

Trade is an essential element of New Zealand’s economic survival.

Taking a neutral stance rather than being dragged into war confrontations among other nations, which do not threaten New Zealand territorial security, should be a priority.

 

 

DEFENCE

New Zealand must retain close military alliance with Australia.

Recognising the reality of military expenditure to equip NZ with evolving technological military developments, New Zealand military should focus on units which provide supply support and reconstruction units.  These units must also be available for recovery and reconstruction of natural disaster events impacting on our Pacific Island neighbours.

Across all services, New Zealand military personnel must (a) attend senior command course in Australia, (b) participate in annual military exercises with Australia.

## Full text (verbatim)

# Press Release

Law & Justice Policy Statement - Improving Access to Justice for Self-Represented Litigants

 

"It is long past time for self-represented litigants navigating the judicial system to be adequately resourced in their endeavours", says Stephen Taylor, Law & Justice Spokesman for the Conservative Party of New Zealand, and a successful self-represented litigant in the Disputes Tribunal, District Court, High Court, Court of Appeal, and the Supreme Court of New Zealand.

In the civil jurisdiction, self-represented litigants make up 71% of the cases on file with court registries throughout New Zealand.

In the New Zealand Family Court, 12.8% of cases involve a self-represented litigant.

In the criminal jurisdiction, just 3% of cases involve a self-represented party, with the Public Defence Service providing the bulk of legal aid assistance (73%) to this group of litigants.

All self-represented litigants across all jurisdictions deserve equal access to justice, however, this is not the case. Too “rich” to qualify for legal aid, but not “rich” enough to be able to afford a lawyer, the burgeoning civil litigant population falls through not just a justice gap, but tumbles into a justice canyon when attempting to secure meaningful access to justice.

Access to justice is a fundamental right, ensuring that every individual can seek and obtain a remedy through the legal system. However, many self-represented litigants face significant barriers, particularly those who do not qualify for legal aid but cannot afford a lawyer.

Mr Taylor proposes a suite of policies to improve access to justice for self-represented litigants across the family, civil, and criminal courts.

1. Proposal for Procedural Improvements

Simplification of Court Forms and Procedures

Simplifying court forms and procedures for self-represented litigants, including providing clear, step-by-step guides and checklists, would reduce the procedural burden on these individuals.

Additionally, offering workshops and training sessions on court processes can empower litigants to handle their cases more effectively.

Not all self-represented litigants are skilled in technology and online navigation, so having simplified documentation would greatly assist this population.

Enhanced Online Resources

Expanding online resources, such as the Ministry of Justice website, to include interactive tools, video tutorials, the development of a single online portal, and comprehensive FAQs can provide self-represented litigants with accessible information and guidance at their convenience.

2. Proposal for Enhanced Support Services

Expansion of Family Legal Advisory Service

The Family Legal Advisory Service provides critical guidance for self-represented litigants in family law matters. Expanding this service to offer more comprehensive support, including detailed procedural advice and assistance with document preparation, would help litigants navigate the complexities of family court proceedings.

This expansion would include additional funding to increase the availability of advisors and extend service hours.

Strengthening Community Law Centres

Community Law Centres offer free legal advice and assistance to those who cannot afford legal representation. Increasing funding for these centres would allow them to hire more staff, including lawyers and paralegals, and extend their outreach programs.

This would ensure that more self-represented litigants receive the necessary support and guidance to pursue their cases effectively.

Enhancement of Kaiārahi Family Court Navigators

Kaiārahi Family Court Navigators assist self-represented litigants by providing information on court procedures and helping them understand their legal rights and obligations. Expanding the navigator program to cover all family court locations and increasing the number of navigators would provide more tailored coaching and resource support to individuals, ensuring they are well-prepared for court appearances.

3. Proposal for Legal Aid Reform

Broadening Legal Aid Eligibility

The eligibility criteria and rates for legal aid in New Zealand need to be increased to catch up with inflation, as the current rates and eligibility thresholds have become long outdated and insufficient.

The Legal Services Agency is mandated to refuse legal aid to applicants whose disposable income or capital exceeds the prescribed thresholds unless there are special circumstances.

These thresholds, such as the maximum disposable capital for civil matters set at $3,500, have not kept pace with inflation and the rising cost of living.

The maximum disposable income thresholds for legal aid eligibility in New Zealand for civil matters are:

$22,366 per year for a single applicant.

$35,420 per year for an applicant with a spouse or partner, or with one dependent child.

$50,934 per year for an applicant with a spouse or partner and one dependent child, or with two dependent children

The current criteria fail to consider the full context of applicants' financial and personal circumstances, which can lead to unjust outcomes. For instance, applicants with disposable capital just above the threshold, despite having significant financial struggles, are often deemed ineligible.

This results in many applicants, who genuinely need legal aid, being denied assistance because their financial situation slightly exceeds these outdated limits.

Therefore, updating the legal aid eligibility criteria and rates to reflect inflation and the actual cost of living would ensure fairer access to justice for all individuals in need.

Flexible Legal Aid Grants

Implementing a more flexible approach to legal aid grants can ensure that individuals who require legal representation but do not meet the strict criteria can still receive support. This includes allowing partial grants or grants for specific stages of the proceedings where self-representation is particularly challenging.

4. Proposal for Pro Bono Scheme Expansion

Compensation for Pro Bono Work

To encourage more lawyers to provide free legal services, the government should introduce:

- A structured scheme offering tax deductions for pro bono work.
- A framework of standard rates to compensate lawyers for pro bono work through awards of costs, reflective of the lawyer's experience and the complexity of the case. Lawyers would be able to invoice clients for work done on a pro bono basis if a costs award is made, ensuring they are compensated for their time and effort.\
 This approach has been recognised as effective in ensuring that pro bono work does not disincentivize legal representation due to the inability to recover costs.

Formalizing Pro Bono Work

Formalizing and expanding the Te Ara Ture pro bono referral service would encourage more lawyers to participate in providing free legal services.

This could include structured programs where lawyers commit to a certain number of pro bono hours annually and receive recognition for their contributions.

5. Expansion of Family Dispute Resolution Service

On 1 July 2025, the Family Dispute Resolution (FDR) service was made free for up to 12 hours. This service is available to parents or guardians involved in disputes regarding the care and contact arrangements for their children, and aims to support children's welfare by facilitating constructive discussions and agreements between parents, ensuring that parents can maintain and strengthen their relationships with their children.

To access the service, individuals must meet specific criteria, including:

- Participation in prescribed programmes under the Domestic Violence Act and the Parenting Through Separation programme.
- Demonstrating a genuine need for mediation to resolve their disputes and being willing to engage in the process cooperatively.

The FDR service supports people to resolve disputes about parenting arrangements without needing to go to court. Removing financial eligibility thresholds for free sessions would encourage people to resolve matters outside of court.

Conclusion

Improving access to justice for self-represented litigants requires a multi-faceted approach, including expanding advisory services, reforming legal aid eligibility, simplifying procedures, enhancing online resources, and improving access to pro bono services.

These measures will ensure that every individual has the support they need to navigate the legal system effectively and fairly.

 

ENDS

# Press Release

#

Law & Justice Policy Statement: Sharpening the Teeth of the IPCA

Further to the concerns raised by the Conservative Party of New Zealand regarding the media-revealed escalation in Police Misconduct, the party's attention now turns to the primary mechanism available to address this escalation - the Independent Police Conduct Authority.

The Independent Police Conduct Authority (IPCA) plays a critical role in maintaining oversight over police conduct and ensuring accountability within the New Zealand Police force.

Given the importance of its functions, it is essential to enhance its capabilities and extend its powers to ensure more effective oversight and accountability.

Proposal for Increased Funding

The IPCA currently operates with the same powers as a Commission of Inquiry, enabling it to summon witnesses, gather evidence, and investigate complaints independently.

However, its effectiveness is often hampered by limited resources.

Whilst the IPCA has around 40 staff and a budget of $5 million a year, these resources are tiny compared to the Police's 14,000 staff and budget of $2.2 billion per year.

Increasing funding for the IPCA would allow it to expand its investigative capacity, reduce delays in processing complaints, and improve its ability to conduct thorough investigations.

This would also enable the IPCA to employ more staff, including legal experts and investigators, to handle the increasing volume of complaints efficiently.

The Conservative Party of New Zealand proposes a doubling of staff and a quadrupling of the annual budget for the IPCA.

Extension of Powers to Sanction and Prosecute

Currently, the IPCA can make recommendations for disciplinary or criminal proceedings but cannot itself lay charges or take disciplinary action.

Extending the IPCA's powers to independently sanction and prosecute police officers for misconduct would significantly enhance its role as an accountability mechanism.

This extension would ensure that the IPCA can take direct action against offending officers, rather than relying on the Police to act on its recommendations.

Empowering the IPCA to prosecute would also serve as a deterrent against misconduct, as individuals would be aware that the authority has the power to enforce consequences.

Given the rise in Police misconduct events and outcomes over recent years, the Conservative Party of New Zealand believes that the extension of these powers is both warranted and overdue.

Power to Name Police Officers Under Investigation

The IPCA can release information on its investigations in the public interest or in the interests of any person.

However, it does not currently have the power to name officers accused of misconduct.

Granting the IPCA the authority to name officers who are under investigation would enhance transparency and public trust.

Naming officers would also hold individuals accountable and prevent them from evading responsibility for their actions.

This measure would encourage higher standards of conduct within the police force and reassure the public that misconduct is being addressed openly and fairly.

The Conservative Party of New Zealand believes that if it is good enough for the Police to publicly name defendants for alleged offenses in the interest of open justice, though they are deemed innocent until proven guilty, then it is good enough for the IPCA to name Police Officers under IPCA investigation for the same reason.

A Truly Independent and Transparent IPCA

The IPCA only independently investigates 2 to 3% of the complaints it receives; the remainder of the complaints are handed back to the Police to investigate themselves, or dismissed by the IPCA at first pass.

With additional staffing and funding as recommended above, it is envisaged that the IPCA will be resourced to conduct more of its investigations, as it is simply not appropriate for a party to an investigation (particularly the Police) to investigate itself.

Despite being a Crown Entity, the IPCA is not subject to the Official Information Act (OIA) — open justice is essential to a free and democratic society, and the Conservative Party of New Zealand recommends legislative change that would submit the IPCA to the OIA.

\
Conclusion

Increasing staffing & funding for the IPCA, extending its powers to independently sanction, prosecute, name offending officers, and enhancing the true independence and transparency of the IPCA would significantly strengthen its ability to oversee police conduct and ensure proper accountability.

These measures are necessary to reverse the declining integrity of the New Zealand Police Force and restore public trust in law enforcement.

 

ENDS

# FamilyBuilder Tax Cuts (2023 policy)

​

Many New Zealanders are struggling with rising costs from high inflation largely due to mismanagement by the government and the Reserve Bank.

At the same time, [tax revenue](https://figure.nz/chart/wNbfI969FfWMnExp) and [government spending](https://figure.nz/chart/8O3m4R92xcJtComx) has roughly doubled over ten years, but taxpayers seem to be getting less value for their money than ever.

It is time to streamline government spending and let New Zealanders keep more of what they earn.

​

Our proposals, outlined below, will give everyone a tax cut, and provide additional tax relief for families with children. They are designed to encourage people to build families and to keep them together.

​

By cutting waste and improving efficiency, government can easily reduce spending by 10%, more than enough to pay for these proposals. ​

## ​

## First $20,000 Tax Free

\
 A tax-free threshold of $20,000 will give everyone a $2,400 tax cut. 

When combined with income splitting, this means a combined $40,000 tax free for a couple, whether one or both spouses are working.

## ​

## ​Income Splitting

New Zealand's progressive tax rates mean, for example, that a family where one parent works 40 hours per week currently pays more tax than a family where both parents work 20 hours and earn the same amount in total. This system penalises families who choose to sacrifice a second income so that one parent can stay home and look after children.

We propose that families with children could divide their income between both parents for tax purposes. This has previously been voted down by both National and Labour, so needs to be pushed by a third party.​

​​

### Child Tax Credits

\
 We propose to implement a $3,000 child tax credit, available to each parent, for a total of $6,000 per child. This would replace the Working for Families "family tax credit" and "in-work tax credit".

​

Together with income splitting, this proposal:

- ​Strengthens families financially.
- Financially discourages fathers from abandoning their families.
- Eliminates frequently raised concerns both by the Left that the "in‑work tax credit" is unfair, and by the Right that abatement rates under Working for Families create a high effective marginal tax rate, which discourages people from taking on an extra job, working overtime, or investing in training and career development.

​​​

Our proposal will provide significant tax relief for many New Zealanders, while ensuring that no one is worse off than under the current system. However, we recognise that under Working for Families, many low-income families already effectively pay no tax—the way to improve things for them is to get inflation under control and grow the economy, providing more job opportunities and higher wages. It is therefore vital for government to reduce unnecessary red tape, and ensure policy encourages people to establish and grow their businesses.

# Our Principles

## Full text (verbatim)

# Our Principles

​

We are a political party in the conservative tradition that seeks to honour the Christian heritage of New Zealand for all who live here.

\
 Our policy and what we stand for is based around the following core principles:​​

​

### 1.  Right to life

Human life is sacred, from conception to natural death. We oppose abortion, euthanasia, and all attacks on innocent human life. 

### 2.  Family

Families are the building blocks of society, so marriage and the family must be supported and strengthened. Strong, stable families enable prosperity, provide security and safety for the vulnerable — including women and children — and transmit values and culture to the next generation.  Government cannot replace the nurturing environment of the family, and must not be allowed to usurp its role.

​

### 3.  Local community

People are created to live in communities, which are necessary for the flourishing of our societies. Decision-making should be as local as possible through a principle known as localism. Society consists of various institutions and communities, including families and religious groups, whose primary authority over their own affairs should be respected and defended. Higher levels of government should serve to empower and support lower levels of authority, rather than control or replace them.

​​

### 4.  Conservation

​

Care for the environment and good stewardship (kaitiakitanga) should characterise the relationship between humanity and creation. Our land and its fruits should benefit all who call New Zealand home. We have a responsibility to protect natural resources, now and for future generations.

​

### 5.  Equal justice

The fundamental role of government is to administer justice and maintain public peace and order. Justice must be equally applied under the law - those who are rich and powerful should not be insulated from the consequences of their actions by a system that makes it impossible for the poor and downtrodden to access justice. Equally, no one should be attacked just because they are rich, and justice cannot favour the poor.

​

The administration of justice must include:​​​

- Punishment that will deter crime.
- Removal of criminals from society, to protect others.
- Recompense and support for victims.
- Genuine rehabilitation.​​​

​Our laws and institutions exist to protect all of us, so must not be weaponised to target people with particular views and to control our lives.

### 6.  Individual Rights and Responsibilities

​

Individuals have a right and a responsibility to provide for and defend themselves and their families. While recognising the need to respond to those who require assistance and compassion, government should promote the prosperity and well-being of the people by facilitating a climate in which:​​​

- Both personal and cooperative initiative is rewarded and excellence is pursued;
- New Zealanders are free to pursue their legitimate self- interest within a competitive economy;
- New Zealanders are free to enjoy the fruits of their labour to the greatest possible extent; and
- Property rights are protected.

​

### 7.  National sovereignty

Parliament has a duty to both maintain national unity and protect the heritage of our distinct communities from agendas that are hostile to our way of life.

​​

​

# Smaller Government

## Full text (verbatim)

# Small Government

​​​​

New Zealand is over-governed, over-regulated, and over-taxed

​

Government is too big and wastes an extraordinary amount of money - and its debt levels are a crisis which needs to be addressed now, or it will strangle our children and grandchildren.\

Much of what government now does is worse than useless - it is harmful to society.   The only solution is to shrink government, so that it focuses on its core business - justice, defence, border control, and critical infrastructure and services.

The more we rely on government, the more control it has over us.  We aim to build back a society where individuals take responsibility for themselves and their own families.

​

Government spending and borrowing are out of control and must be slashed

The current government was elected with a strong mandate to slash red tape and reduce government spending - which had doubled over just a decade.  But despite such substantial efforts as creating a whole new Ministry for Regulation (employing yet another tribe of well-paid bureaucrats), its main achievements include:

- continuing to spend even more than Labour, [locking in "big government" programs such as school lunches](https://www.conservatives.nz/news/when-government-plays-socialist-games-it-wins-socialist-prizes),
- [doubling down on the economic sabotage of “net zero” climate policy,](https://www.taxpayers.org.nz/climate_targets) and
- reducing requirements for road cones!

​

The problem is clearly ‘baked in’ to the system, and radical change is needed.   We do not need Big Government done better.

The ever expanding power of government must be reversed

​

The growth in spending is largely because we have become ever more dependent on government, and allowed it to take over more and more of our lives.  Society works best when people are responsible for their own lives and free to decide how to run their own households and businesses.  Our people should be treated as adults - trusted and expected to spend their own money and provide for themselves and their families.

\
 We need more than platitudes and token reforms - the problems are deep-rooted and systemic.\
 Overseas leaders have shown us that government doesn’t need to constantly grow – its spending, its borrowing, and its control over our lives.

\
 All that is needed is a mindset change.  The Conservatives offer that change. We will:

- [Legislate to curtail unconstitutional bureaucratic power](https://www.conservatives.nz/news/has-new-zealand-lost-control-of-its-own-government).
- Radically reduce government by abolishing useless government agencies and programs and ending wasteful spending and unnecessary regulation.
- Get the government’s fingers out of our lunchboxes and wallets.
- Restore rational economic policy, including [ending all climate-focused taxes, subsidies, and regulations](https://www.conservatives.nz/environment).
- Reform the welfare system (including Working For Families - to be replaced by our [FamilyBuilder](https://www.conservatives.nz/familybuilder-old) tax cuts) and education (including ECE), to make sure it [supports the family](https://www.conservatives.nz/family) instead of undermining it.
- End all forms of corporate welfare including subsidies for the media.
- End the gravy train for public servants, consultants, tribal elites and politicians.
- Re-direct spending towards critical services and infrastructure, including roads, bridges and waterways.
- Review major infrastructure projects for viability and to ensure they deliver real benefits and are completed on time and within budget.

​

Everyday New Zealanders have to work hard to balance their books, and they need government to do the same.  We will regularly review current expenditure (day-to-day government spending, which dwarfs capital expenditure), with a view to reducing costs.  This should be a constant and healthy practice of all governments - just as it is for families and businesses.

​

If we learn anything from the covid years, it should be that government is not God.  We cannot expect it to solve all our problems, and we mustn't allow it to control how we live our lives.

​

Vote to end the disaster of Big Government.  Vote Conservative.
